title: Area between curves
examples: How do I find the area if the curves cross over?
What do I do if the limits are given by the intersection points?
Is it always top minus bottom when calculating this area?

explain.say: Today we learn to find the area between two curves. We use definite integrals for this calculation. Think of it like finding the space trapped between two lines or shapes.
The first step is always finding the intersection points. These points set the boundaries for our area calculation. We set the two functions equal to each other to find these x values.

Next, we must determine which function is the top curve. We test a point between the intersection points to see which function has the greater y value. This is crucial for setting up the integral correctly.

The formula for the area is the integral of the top function minus the bottom function. We use the intersection points as our limits of integration. Remember the structure: integral from a to b of (Top - Bottom) dx.

faq.q: What if the curves intersect more than twice?
faq.a: You must calculate the area in separate sections. You find the intersections, and then you calculate the area for each enclosed region individually. You add up all these separate areas at the end.
asks: How many areas do I calculate?
Do I need separate integrals for each overlap?

faq.q: Do I always integrate with respect to x?
faq.a: No, sometimes you must integrate with respect to y. This means you need to rewrite your functions in terms of y. You then integrate the right function minus the left function.
asks: What if I use dy instead of dx?
When should I switch to integrating with respect to y?

faq.q: Can I just use the difference of the functions without integrating?
faq.a: No, you cannot simply subtract the functions. The area calculation requires finding the definite integral of the difference. The integral sums up the small vertical slices of area.
asks: Why do I need the integral sign?

faq.q: What are the limits of integration if they are not given?
faq.a: If the limits are not given, they are the x coordinates where the two curves intersect. You find these by setting the equations equal to each other.
asks: Do I solve for x when finding the limits?

faq.q: Does the order of subtraction matter?
faq.a: Yes, the order matters greatly. You must always subtract the lower function from the upper function. If you reverse the order, you will get a negative area value.
asks: If I swap the order, what happens?

facts: The area between two curves is found using definite integration.
The general setup is the integral from the left limit to the right limit.
The integrand must be the top function minus the bottom function.
Intersection points determine the limits of integration for the area.

quiz.say: Find the area between y = x and y = x^2 from x = 0 to x = 1.
quiz.why: The line y = x is always above the parabola y = x squared in this interval, so we calculate the integral of x minus x squared.

wrong.0: This is the result of integrating only the top function, x, and ignoring the bottom function.
wrong.1: This is incorrect because the area is clearly positive in the first quadrant.
wrong.3: This is the result of integrating x minus x squared but forgetting to evaluate the constant term correctly.

quiz.say: If the intersection points are at x = -1 and x = 1, and f(x) is on top, what is the integral setup?
quiz.why: The limits of integration are the intersection points, and the integrand must be the top function minus the bottom function.

wrong.0: This reverses the subtraction order, which will yield the negative of the actual area.
wrong.1: This only calculates the vertical distance at one point, not the accumulated area over the interval.
wrong.3: This incorrectly assumes the limits are zero and one, ignoring the actual intersection points.

quiz.say: To find the area bounded by y = x and y = x^2, what is the correct integral setup?
quiz.why: The intersection points are 0 and 1, and for this interval, x is the top function and x squared is the bottom function.

wrong.1: This reverses the order, calculating the negative of the true area.
wrong.2: While mathematically equivalent, the standard form combines this into one integral for simplicity.
wrong.3: This is just the expression, not the definite integral required to find the total area.
